title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6771 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: ECB bond market intervention warning from Governor Knot. Can't replace sound fiscal policy,
body: Knot's line on fiscal discipline matters most for euro zone sovereign spreads, especially French bonds against German Bunds. Markets will read it as a reminder that ECB support would be conditional rather than open-ended. A president with that view could make investors less willing to bet on a full central bank backstop if French finances get worse, which risks wider spreads during periods of stress. On rates, his cautious, data-driven stance on energy-driven inflation is softer than the hike signals coming from more hawkish policymakers, so a Knot presidency would lean toward patience rather than front-loaded tightening. title: ICYMI - Trump extends Jones Act waiver 90 days, foreign tankers moving oil in US
body: For oil, the extension is a small but useful relief valve rather than a supply story. It does not add barrels to the market, but it moves them more efficiently between US regions. The fact that most of the extra volume has been refined products suggests the main effect is on product cracks and regional spreads rather than on benchmark crude. Since the administration is still relying on emergency measures like this, traders should take it as a sign that Washington does not expect fuel prices tied to the Iran war to ease soon. --- Earlier: Iran says supertanker with 2 million barrels sank after Hormuz mine strike, unconfirmed --- Washington has again set aside a century-old shipping protection in the name of cheaper fuel, a sign that the Iran war's pressure on gasoline and diesel prices is still running ahead of political sensitivities over shipbuilding. Summary: President Trump extended a waiver of the Jones Act for 90 days, letting foreign-flagged ships carry oil and commodities between US ports. Moreover, Trump stated on Truth Social that the US doesn't need a deal with Iran, triggering a rally in oil prices and the US dollar. Looking ahead, I would expect rate hikes to start putting significant downward pressure on the stock market and long-term Treasury yields amid increased growth concerns given the longer than expected US-Iran tensions. I think that in the current context, if Trump decides to escalate things with Iran, inflation expectations would rise alongside a weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. And this should ultimately be bullish for gold. At the same time, if we get a de-escalation, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term. There are certainly strong headwinds for gold at the moment, so these fundamental views will need to be paired with technicals for a confirmation of a change in momentum.

title: AI: Daily quotas come to DeepSeek, a visible sign of China's AI chip crunch
body: For investors, the DeepSeek report is a live data point in the debate over AI computing power. It suggests demand at China's leading AI lab is running ahead of the chips it can get. Paired with the US plans to curb remote access in Southeast Asia, that could support the case for China's domestic chipmakers and AI infrastructure suppliers. It also raises questions over how fast Chinese platforms can grow their AI services. For Nvidia, ahead of Tuesday's results, it underlines how much Chinese demand is still unmet, and how much of it depends on routes Washington may now close. Until DeepSeek confirms the changes, markets are likely to treat this as a signal rather than a catalyst. --- China's best-known AI lab is rationing its free chatbot for lack of computing power, a rare public glimpse of the chip squeeze that US export controls were designed to create. Summary: DeepSeek has restricted use of its app and web service, citing insufficient computing power, according to multiple user reports. Long conversations inactive for over seven days are no longer supported, and single inputs are capped at about 40,000 characters. Daily conversation quotas have been introduced. Users who hit the cap see a "server congestion" message. DeepSeek had not previously published a daily cap for its free chat. In May it quietly limited the regenerate and edit functions. The company has not issued a public statement.

title: BOJ's Takata calls for nimble hikes after 1.5% bid, says neutral rate may top estimates
body: Takata's speech is the clearest public argument yet for a faster BOJ hiking pace than markets assume. He rejects a fixed quarterly rhythm and argues for reaching the middle of the neutral range early, which puts a move beyond 1.5% within view. Because his views are his own and he has been outvoted, it doesn't change December pricing by itself. But it supports the yen and adds upward pressure on front-end JGB yields, especially with USD/JPY near 160. His explicit link between real rate differentials and the currency also signals that BOJ hawks see rate hikes as a tool against yen weakness. On the same day as a weak GDP print, the debate on the board is now plainly about speed, not direction. --- Takata wants the BOJ to stop hiking on a timetable and start hiking on the data, and with producer prices running at 7% and the yen near 160, he thinks the data already argues for moving faster. Summary: BOJ board member Hajime Takata said 2026 is a regime change, requiring nimble, data-dependent rate hikes rather than a fixed pace. He laid out the case for his October proposal to raise the policy rate to 1.5% from 1.25%, and stressed that the views are his own. He said underlying inflation has reached 2%, inflation expectations are above 2% and producer prices rose 7.1% in October. He said Japan's neutral rate could exceed market expectations, and the BOJ should move early towards the middle of the estimated 1.1% to 2.5% range.

title: China's October data shows the economy losing momentum on retail sales and industry output

title: Natural gas analysis with the "perfect" trading range
body: Natural gas has a beautiful trading range. Where's the easy entry? Natural gas futures have repeatedly approached $2.50 and $3.40, creating an almost textbook trading range. But Monday's weakness highlights why an attractive chart pattern does not automatically produce an attractive trade. The $3.20-$3.24 area is now the immediate test. The daily chart of NYMEX natural gas futures (NG1!) presents something traders love to see: an apparently well-defined trading range, with a floor around $2.50 and a ceiling near $3.40. It looks almost too good to be true. And that brings us to an important lesson: Knowing where a market might reverse is not the same as knowing when, or whether, to trade that reversal. The trading range looks remarkably precise On the continuous futures chart, natural gas reached $2.495 on April 24 and $2.497 on October 26. That's a difference of just $0.002 per MMBtu. At the upper boundary, the June 1 high of $3.396 was almost identical to the November 11 high of $3.397. Those matching extremes create an appealing picture of buyers defending the lower boundary and sellers resisting the upper one. But the latest price action provides an important reality check. Natural gas reached $3.397 on November 11, retreated, recovered to close at $3.361 on November 12, and then fell to $3.242 on November 13. On Monday, November 16, the developing daily candle opened at $3.180. Its observed high was just $3.192, below Friday's $3.206 low.

title: Fed's Warsh doesn't talk about monetary policy in a speech on AI
body: Warsh delivered comments at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco and there's nothing market-moving in them. Highlights of the speech: Calls the current era possibly "the most transformational period in my adult lifetime" AI (he calls it SI) "could supercharge idea generation" and sustain growth substantially above the long-run average Productivity growth has been "reasonably strong" in recent quarters but hasn't yet broken out "definitively and structurally to the upside" The Fed's role is "neither advocacy nor opposition" Widespread adoption will have "important implications for monetary policy down the road" "We're certainly not here to make predictions" Board staff has begun modelling scenarios; they're "illustrative scenarios, not forecasts" Flags risks to critical infrastructure, saying SI "empowers all, including bad actors" "Can you be a superpower without super intelligence?" If you were looking for a hint on the next move in rates, there's nothing here. The only mention of monetary policy is that one line about implications "down the road". There's nothing on inflation, the neutral rate or the balance sheet. What you do get is a look at how the Fed is framing the AI question. The staff scenarios are: Productivity rises, the gains are shared between labor and capital, GDP growth runs persistently above trend and the economy stays near full employment.

title: Tiff Macklem should have been fired, not celebrated
body: Tiff Macklem announced that he will retire after his seven-year term ends in June 2027. He should have left much sooner. It continues to baffle me that no central banker paid the price for the disastrous covid inflation. In no other high-profile field in the world is incompetence tolerated to the extent it is in central banking. It's a field that's protected both by government independence and a culture that accepts failure. No one exemplified that more than Tiff Macklem and his performance during the pandemic. Despite a raging housing bubble, his bank cut rates to 0.25% in the pandemic. On its own, that's forgivable given the pandemic uncertainty, layoffs and a once-in-a-generation public health event. Where it went off the rails was with forward guidance that destroyed the central bank's credibility, supercharged the housing bubble, sparked devastating inflation and then led to the subsequent housing crash. The single individual most responsible for all of that was Tiff Macklem, and yet no one inside or outside the central banking community called for accountability. The worst of his sins was the infamous line that he should forever be remembered by: "If you've got a mortgage, or you're considering to make a major purchase... you can be confident that interest rates will be low for a long time," he said on July 15, 2020. "Interest rates are very low and they are going to be there for a long time," he added. Critically, the assurance was unqualified and unconditional.

title: Forget the petro-dollar, introducing the chip-dollar
body: Deutsche Bank's Mallika Sachdeva is out with a big-picture note arguing that semiconductors have quietly become one of the most important drivers of the US dollar. The headline stat is a stunner: for the first time in modern history, global trade in semiconductors exceeds trade in oil and gas. That's based on the four quarters through Q2 2026. More important for FX is where the surpluses are piling up. Chip surpluses in Asia ex-China (Korea, Taiwan, Japan and ASEAN) have now caught up to the petroleum surpluses in the Gulf. For 50 years the deal was simple: the Gulf sold oil in dollars and recycled the proceeds into Treasuries. Deutsche argues that regime is being superseded, and rather quickly. The difference this time is where the money goes. Korea is the case study: Semiconductor exports are up more than 200% y/y this year The chip trade surplus is close to $250 billion Chips account for 100% of Korea's overall trade surplus Korean purchases of overseas equities have been five times purchases of overseas bonds over the past two years 70% of Korea's overseas equity holdings are in the US, and it's 90% for Korean households So the chip money is going straight back into the US tech companies that are buying the chips.

title: Goldman Sachs gets bearish on oil prices but doesn't see help for consumers
body: Goldman Sachs is out with its 2027 oil outlook and the title says it all: "Adaptation." The theme is that crude prices ran well above pre-war expectations this year, but not nearly as high as you would have guessed if you'd known how long the Hormuz disruptions would last. Mideast supply and global demand both adjusted better than anyone anticipated. Their forecasts Brent to average $88/bbl in 2027 (spot at $94.11) Easing to $78/bbl by December 2027 Fair value falls from $90/bbl today as the market returns to surplus US wholesale diesel to average $150/bbl in 2027 The supply side is where it gets interesting. Goldman's base case has Mideast supply rising above its 2025 average next year, thanks to ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions, while supply growth elsewhere stalls. The real story might be in products. Goldman sees crude normalizing but products staying well above average for three reasons: Slow net refining capacity growth keeps product markets structurally tight The Mideast conflict continues to support product prices through low exports, high freight rates and deferred maintenance Russian product output is assumed to remain largely constrained That's a world where the headline crude price tells you less and less about what consumers and businesses are paying. Diesel at $150 is a tax on everything that moves, but it's good news for refiners. Note though that the CRAK refiners ETF has come down in the past month.

body: Prior was +25.50 Full report The New York Fed's Empire State Manufacturing Index fell 18 points to 7.8 in November, remaining in expansionary territory but signalling a loss of momentum following October's strong increase. New orders and shipments continued to grow modestly, while unfilled orders increased and delivery times lengthened. Inventories also moved higher, although supply availability remained constrained. The labour market indicators strengthened significantly. The employment index jumped to 18.1, its highest level since June 2022, while the average workweek index rose to 13.5, pointing to stronger hiring and longer working hours. On the inflation front, price pressures moderated but remained elevated. The prices paid index fell 14 points to 45.9, while the prices received index edged down to 27.2, suggesting a slower pace of increases in both input and selling prices. Looking ahead, firms became more optimistic about the outlook. The future business conditions index rose eight points to 28.9, while the capital expenditures index climbed to 23.0, its highest level since December 2022. The data points to continued manufacturing expansion in New York, supported by stronger employment and investment intentions, although activity has cooled from October and cost pressures remain elevated. title: Why the AI trade is a macro trade: the risks to the US economy
body: The massive investment required to develop AI infrastructure has become an increasingly important driver of US economic growth, while also influencing inflation and interest rates. This means that the US economy has become vulnerable to a slowdown in this investment cycle. The development of AI has required enormous capital expenditure. Hyperscalers and technology companies have been investing heavily in data centres, semiconductors, networking equipment and electricity infrastructure. This spending has supported economic activity through several channels. It contributed to business investment, created demand for industrial goods and construction services, supported employment and generated revenues across a wide supply chain. There is also a financial market channel. Strong expectations for AI-related earnings have supported the stock market, leading to a positive wealth effect and increasing confidence and consumption. The US economy has therefore become increasingly leveraged to the AI investment cycle. As long as companies continue increasing capital expenditure, corporate earnings improve and equity valuations remain supported. However, if expected returns on AI investment disappoint, companies could reduce spending, affecting suppliers, employment and broader business activity. A prolonged bear market in AI-related stocks could amplify the impact through the wealth effect.

title: FX option expiries for 16 November 10am New York cut
body: EUR/USD 1.1200 (EUR 1.48 bn) 1.1100 (EUR 1.18 bn) USD/JPY 160.00 (US$ 1.52 bn) 159.00 (US$ 1.24 bn) GBP/USD 1.3200 (GBP 564.00 mn) USD/CHF 0.8400 (US$ 634.73 mn) USD/CAD 1.4310 (US$ 334.27 mn) 1.4110 (US$ 500.08 mn) AUD/USD 0.6920 (AUD 409.38 mn) What are FX option expiries? The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts. When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET). Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on). As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Crude oil remains supported amid the prolonged US-Iran standoff and risks of military escalation
body: Crude oil has been bottoming out near the 87.00 handle as the market realised that the US-Iran standoff may drag on longer than expected, with the additional risk that Trump decides to pursue another military campaign. As a reminder, the culprit for the increase in prices was Trump's post on Truth Social stating that the US doesn't need a deal with Iran. Moreover, Trump warned that the US would not hesitate to take further military action if current measures fail to achieve objectives. According to Axios, the USS Roosevelt has arrived in the Middle East with the aircraft carrier joining two others operating in the CENTCOM area. Meanwhile, Iran targeted a military base in Bahrain with six drones, marking its first direct strike on the country in several weeks. Moreover, Iran reported multiple tanker incidents involving naval mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, warning oil companies that parts of the southern shipping route remain mined and that vessels cooperating with US forces risk coming under fire. Finally, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson ruled out suspending uranium enrichment activities or reducing enrichment levels. It goes without saying that a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly. But as of now, this scenario looks much less probable.

title: What Does Big Tech's AI Spending Tell Us About Nvidia's Sales?

Its next-quarter sales, however, also depend on how much equipment it can deliver. Nvidia reports on 17 November for its fiscal third quarter, which ended on 25 October 2026. The cloud providers' September results offer evidence about an overlapping period. Their spending plans look further ahead, helping traders assess whether investment is likely to continue beyond the quarter Nvidia is about to report. body: Neither release is likely to move the New Zealand dollar much on its own. The Financial Stability Report assesses risk rather than signalling policy, and the food price data is only a small input into quarterly inflation. Its list of global risks, from Middle East energy disruption to an AI valuation correction, reads like a list of the shocks that tend to hurt risk-sensitive currencies like the kiwi. --- Coming up later from neighbouring Australia: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock --- New Zealand food prices fell in October. title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock
body: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock is due to speak from 9.50am Sydney time (2250 GMT, 1750 US Eastern on Monday). She is appearing at the ASIC Annual Forum alongside other regulators. The minutes of the November meeting follow at 11.30am Sydney time (0030 GMT/1930 US Eastern time). The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, its highest level since November 2008 and the fifth increase of 2026. Six board members voted for the hike and three wanted to hold at 4.60%. That split is why the minutes matter more than usual. Analysts will look at how the minutes describe the balance of risks between inflation and economic activity, whether the minority thought policy was already restrictive enough, and how high the bar is for further hikes. The RBA's own assessment puts the current cash rate slightly above the top of its range of neutral rate estimates. It also sees inflation staying above 3% until late 2027. Markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December hike. Bullock's remarks will be watched for any sign that persistent inflation and high capacity pressures could justify another increase. Any such signal would push back against that pricing. Market impact: The Australian dollar has taken the hit from the repricing. It was trading at around 67.6 US cents late on Monday after earlier falling to its lowest level since late January. If either the speech or the minutes leans hawkish, AUD/USD and short-dated yields could get support.

title: Hammack: Economy can handle more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go
body: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack spoke with Bloomberg: Goes into all FOMC meetings with open mind There is not much tension between Fed mandates, inflation going in wrong direction Preference has been for steady, slow rate hike increments 'I like moving in smaller increments' to allow economy to adjust to policy changes Inflation pressures appear to be broadening Worried businesses are more accepting of price rises Businesses are passing on more price increases Job market has been largely in balance, but is not dynamic Will continue to express viewpoints With AI, range of impact is very wide Definitely seeing inflation pressures from tech investment Doesn't see AI investment creating issues for government borrowing costs Higher market borrowing costs needed to restrain economy Financial conditions are still not restraining the economy The economy can deal with more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go 2% inflation is still a reasonable goal for the Fed Hammack lines up squarely with the Logan-Daly camp and adds the most direct conditions-based argument yet: financial conditions "still not restraining the economy" and higher borrowing costs are "needed" — the mirror image of Bowman's tightening-has-done-work framing. "The economy can deal with more restriction" is a green light for hikes; "unclear how far the Fed has to go" leaves the terminal rate open-ended, which is the more hawkish read.
